newsitem.title: GERMANY: TENNIS-GERMANY STARTS HUNT FOR NEW BORIS OR STEFFI.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-GERMANY STARTS HUNT FOR NEW BORIS OR STEFFI.

text.p: German tennis, down in the doldrums with big names Steffi Graf and Michael Stich plagued by injury, is looking for a new Boris Becker.
As Becker prepares for one of his final attempts to reclaim the Wimbledon championship he last won in 1989, the search has begun in Germany for a new generation of tennis greats.
The shock triumph of the lanky 17-year-old at Wimbledon in 1985 sparked a German tennis boom and wealthy sponsors do not want interest in the sport to die with the end of his career.
They have even found themselves a new Boris -- Boris Bachert -- a 16-year-old redhead from Becker's home town.

The beginning of the end of the Becker-Stich-Graf era hit home only when Stich announced last month he would retire at the end of this season. Graf sent out more shockwaves this week when she said she was also considering ending her career.

Graf, who celebrated her 28th birthday last Saturday in a physiotherapy clinic where she is recovering from an operation on her knee, will not be able to defend either her Wimbledon or her U.S. Open title this year.

Stich, who has fallen back to 89th in the world -- his worst ranking since the end of 1989 -- said he would retire later in the year because of a nagging shoulder injury. The 1991 Wimbledon champion has failed to perform well since he reached the French Open final last year.
Becker too is feeling the strain, his world ranking slipping to 18 from 13 after he lost in the semifinals of the Halle grasscourt tournament in the build-up to his 14th consecutive Wimbledon.
The 29-year-old has also been plagued by injury but last month said he was not about to follow Stich out of the game and hoped to play for another two or three years.

Tennis officials say it will be hard to replace Boris and Steffi in the hearts of Germans, who enjoyed watching the two grow up -- Becker into a doting father and Graf into a model who has promoted everything from pasta to deodorant.

"It would be difficult to find a new Steffi or Boris because they were both exceptions. But we need new players in the top 10 or 20 to keep interest high," said Jens-Peter Hecht, spokesman for the German Tennis Federation (DTB).
Becker has decided to find his own successor and approached one of his sponsors, German luxury carmaker Mercedes-Benz, to find the money to launch a new junior men's team.

"Everybody has been too laid back in the last few years... It was only when Michael (Stich) and I were missing at the French Open that you saw the reality. The situation must be improved," Becker said last week.
Mercedes-Benz, which already pours money into sponsoring 72 ATP tournaments around the world, has set aside an extra 40 million marks over the next 10 years for Becker's team.
Between four and six youngsters will be chosen next month and trained by Becker, Klaus Langenbach and Klaus Hofsaess, trainer of the German women's team since 1984.

"I am sure I can pass on a lot of things to the young players... They must be able to cope with great triumph as well as painful defeat," Becker said. "The exhausting vagabond life of the tennis circuit has just as many problems and impact on success as knowing how to hit the ball."

Two youngsters are already sure of their places in the elite squad: Alex Radulescu, 22 and Nicholas Kiefer, a 19-year-old who won this year's junior Australian Open. The two will be among 12 German men at this year's Wimbledon.

"I made it into the world top 60 with my own efforts. Perhaps Boris Becker can help me get higher and reach the limits of my potential with his experience and knowledge," said Radulescu, who has recently slipped back to 63 in the rankings.

The remaining places in the squad will be taken by younger players. Among the hopefuls are Philipp Hammer, 16, and Daniel Leske, 15, who have both trained with Becker recently in Monte Carlo, where the teenage Becker started his career with former manager Ion Tiriac.
But it is 16-year-old Boris Bachert from Becker's hometown of Leimen near Frankfurt who has attracted all the headlines.
Bachert, who is German champion for his age group, is said to have a similar strength of forehand and service and should be as tall as the older Boris when he stops growing.
When the old master met Bachert he was amazed.

"When I saw this young tennis player I thought this cannot be true! He looks like I did at 16, has the same build as I did then, plays like I did then, talks as I did and even comes from Leimen," Becker exclaimed.

The chances are bleak for a similar women's elite squad. Hofsaess, moving from the women's team to coach Becker's boys, said such a team would never work because of the intense rivalry between parents pushing their daughters to the top.
Sources close to the DTB have said Graf has even considered taking over Hofsaess's position as women's trainer.

Graf, who has fallen to world number three after a brief and disappointing return to court following three months out with injury, said last weekend one of the reasons she did not want to rush a comeback was to be sure she could remain active after her playing career ended.

World number eight Anke Huber, 22, is one favourite to take over the Graf mantle but she disappointed fans when she went out in the first round of the French Open. She is the highest seeded German woman of six at this year's Wimbledon.
The race to find a new Boris or Steffi is not just a matter of national pride but vital for the whole business of tennis, with German sponsors funding many of the main tournaments.

The successes of Graf and Becker fuelled massive interest in the sport in Germany in the 1980s, with the men's game bringing two of the most important tournaments -- the ATP world championship and the Grand Slam Cup -- to the country.

Germany also hosts an array of big women's and men's tournaments throughout the year and has the facilities for producing players with its abundance of indoor courts and extensive training programme for youngsters.
"Lots of money comes from the German sponsors and if they were to withdraw, it wouldn't just affect German tennis but tennis as a whole," Hecht said.
